subject: Communication
title: Listening Up: How Leaders Hear Dissent
description: One-minute skill: Listening Up: How Leaders Hear Dissent.

hook.text: A CEO asks for honest feedback. Everyone says 'great job.' Is the work really that good — or is everyone too afraid to speak?

buildup.text: Power dynamics filter what leaders hear. Subordinates self-censor, sugarcoat, and tell leaders what they want to hear.

discovery.text: Ethan Burris found that leaders who actively seek dissent and thank dissenters receive 40% more useful information.

twist.text: The first time a leader punishes dissent, it takes months to rebuild the willingness to speak up.

climax.text: The best leaders create 'safe to fail' zones: regular forums where critical feedback is expected, welcomed, and acted upon.

punchline.text: If everyone agrees with the leader, the leader isn't listening hard enough.

quiz.question: How much more useful information do leaders who actively seek dissent receive?

details.summary: Leaders who actively seek and listen to dissenting opinions make better decisions. But hierarchy naturally suppresses bad news and disagreement. Creating conditions where people feel safe to speak up, and then genuinely hearing them, is the hardest and most important leadership listening skill.
details.whyItMatters: Organizations fail when leaders cannot hear uncomfortable truths. The ability to listen up separates great leaders from those surrounded by yes-people.
takeaways: Hierarchy suppresses dissent and uncomfortable truths
Leaders must actively create space for contrary views
Listening to dissent prevents groupthink and blind spots

faq.question: Why do leaders struggle to hear dissent?
faq.answer: Power changes the brain, reducing empathy and perspective-taking. Leaders receive filtered information because subordinates fear consequences of honesty. Success reinforces confidence in current approaches. The combination creates information bubbles that insulate leaders from reality.

faq.question: How can leaders signal that they genuinely want dissent?
faq.answer: Publicly thank people who disagree. Never punish bad news, even subtly. Share your own uncertainties and mistakes. Assign someone to argue the opposing position. Follow up on concerns raised. If people see that dissent is rewarded, not punished, they will speak honestly.
